(1) The realm of nature (ʿālam al-ṭabīʿa), which is the worldly domain (dunyā) we inhabit. The entities within it are material forms that operate according to principles of motion, stillness, change, and transformation.

(2) The realm of archetypes (ʿālam al-mithāl), which exists above the realm of nature. It contains forms of things without any material substance, from which natural events descend and to which they return. This realm has a superior standing and causative relationship to the events of the natural world.

(3) The realm of intellect (ʿālam al-ʿaql), which is situated above the realm of exemplars. W ithin it lie the realities of entities and their universals, devoid of any natural substance or form. It has a causative relationship to what exists in the realm of exemplars. Given the human soul’s immaterial nature, it resonates with both the realm of exemplars and the realm of intellect. W hen a person sleeps and the senses are dormant, the soul naturally detaches from external natural matters and reverts to its resonating realm, witnessing some of its truths, contingent upon its readiness and capability.

If the soul is complete and adept at grasping abstract intellectual entities, it perceives and brings forth the causes of entities in their universality

and luminosity. Otherwise, it narrates them in an imaginative manner, relating to the forms and cosmic particularities it is familiar with, just as we

convey the concept of speed through the image of a fast-moving object, the concept of greatness via a mountain, the concept of elevation and loftiness through the sky and its celestial bodies, cunningness and deceit through a fox, envy through a wolf, bravery through a lion, and so forth.

If the soul is not capable of comprehending abstracts as they are and ascending to their realm, it halts in the realm of exemplars, having ascended from the realm of nature. It may then witness events by observing their causes and reasons without actively intervening or altering anything. This often occurs in souls that are pure and characterized by truthfulness and clarity; these are termed as clear dreams (manāmāt ṣarīḥa).

At times, the soul may relate what it has seen using familiar metaphors and symbols, such as representing marriage with putting on items of clothing, honor with a crown, knowledge with light, ignorance with darkness,

and the extinguishing of memory with death. Sometimes we transition from one opposite to another, as our minds shift from the concept of poverty when hearing of wealth, from the image of fire to that office, or from the concept of life to that of death, and so on. An example of this type of dream was recounted where a man saw in his dream that he had a seal with which he sealed people’s mouths and private parts. When he asked Ibn Sīrīn for its interpretation, he replied: ‘You will become a caller to

prayer in the month of Ramaḍān, and people will fast based on your call.’ From the above discussion, it becomes clear that true dreams can be primarily divided into two categories: clear dreams (manāmāt ṣarīḥa) where

the sleeping soul has not intervened, which can be interpreted directly without any hindrance, and unclear dreams (manāmāt ghayr ṣarīḥa) where the soul intervenes by narrating through metaphors and transitioning from one meaning to its counterpart or its opposite. These require interpretation by referring back to the higher principle that the soul first observed

and translated into an image, like relating the crown back to pride, death back to life, life back to relief after hardship, darkness to ignorance, confusion, or misery.

The second category further divides into two subcategories. The first is where the soul narrates and moves from one thing to its counterpart or its opposite, perhaps once or twice, making it relatively easy to revert back to its primary meaning, as exemplified earlier. The second is where the soul narrates without any fixed reference, transitioning, for instance, from one thing to its opposite, then from the opposite to something similar, and from the likeness of the opposite to its counter-opposite, and so

on. This makes it challenging or impossible for the interpreter to trace back to the original vision. These types of dreams are termed ‘confused dreams’ (aḍghāth al-aḥlām) and are usually not interpretable due to their complexity or ambiguity.

Thus, it becomes evident that dreams can be classified into three main categories: clear dreams (manāmāt ṣarīḥa) that do not require interpretation due to their straightforward nature, confused dreams (aḍghāth

al-aḥlām) that are not interpretable due to their complexity, and dreams where the soul narrates with metaphors and symbolic representations, which are interpretable.

The summarizes what the ancient scholars of the soul (ʿulamāʾ al-nafs) have discussed about dreams and their in-depth investigation. Readers requiring further details can refer to the texts they have written on this subject.

Support for this in the Qurʾan:

There is evidence that supports this notion found in the Qurʾan. For example, God says: It is He who takes your souls by night (6:60). He also states: Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those who have not died in their sleep. Then He retains those for whom He has ordained death and releases the others until a specified time (39:42). The apparent meaning is that souls are taken away and separated from their bodies, disconnected from the physical senses, and return to their Lord in a manner

that is analogous to death.

W ithin the Qurʾanic discourse, references can be found to each of the three aforementioned categories of dreams. From the first category, we have examples like the vision of Abraham, the vision of the mother of Moses, and some of the visions of the Prophet Muḥammad. From the second category, there is the verse: They said, ‘Confused nightmares, and we do not know the interpretation of nightmares’ (12:44). From the third category, there are Joseph’s dreams, the dreams of his two prison companions, and the dream of the Egyptian king, all of which are mentioned in

the chapter of Joseph.
